h: Rugby league roots and Pennine adventures
p: Huddersfield is a proud town with a few claims to fame. Back in 1895, a meeting at the George Hotel in St George's Square led to the birth of what became rugby league, and the town is still known as its birthplace. Just across the square, the railway station is a real showpiece, with a magnificent classical frontage that looks more like a stately home than a ticket office. A statue of Harold Wilson, the former prime minister born in the town, stands outside.

For the inflatables themselves, it helps to plan around energy levels. Little ones might want a slower start before they're brave enough for the big slides, while older kids will race straight to the toughest obstacles. Agree a meeting point inside before you set off, and keep the drinks handy. Afterwards everyone will be peckish, so it's worth having a plan for food rather than wandering round looking hungry.

If you've got the rest of the day, the countryside is right on the doorstep. Holmfirth, a short drive south, is famous as the setting for Last of the Summer Wine and has cafes, independent shops and pretty streets to explore. The Huddersfield Narrow Canal heads west towards the Pennines and the Standedge Tunnel, where boat trips take you into the hill and a visitor centre tells its story. On a clear day, the moors around Marsden are perfect for blowing away the cobwebs. Pack a waterproof though, because Pennine weather has a mind of its own. Back in town, the market hall and the streets around the station have plenty of spots for a warming brew.
